title: What Else Do I Need to Know About Cognitive Science?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: This is a chapter-style run through cognitive science findings that Salles thinks English teachers need, each paired with a quoted passage from the research and an explicit implication for classroom practice. He covers the generation effect, students' mistaken belief that massed practice works better than spacing, working memory limits, dual coding, mind maps and elaboration. His central move is translation: for each finding he says what it changes in how students make revision notes, how teachers present text, and how mock exams should be used. The sharpest implication is that mocks are over-trusted, and that re-sitting the same questions weeks later teaches more than the mock itself. The piece is practical and opinionated, though it leans on quoted studies and on his own experience rather than new evidence.
points: Generation tasks such as anagrams and first-letter cues improve memory of a whole essay, not just the cued words.
Students and teachers wrongly trust massed practice and mocks, so spaced re-testing of the same questions gives a truer picture of learning.
Because speech and writing share one channel, teachers should stop talking while students read and should limit new information to about four chunks.
Labelled diagrams help working memory, while decorative pictures do not.
Elaboration works only if students do it themselves, so the instruction has to be written into their booklets as a task.
quotes: Implication – we believe that mock exams are an effective way to prepare students for exams. They revise for the mock, and then they practise the questions – it makes sense. But while this is better than not revising and not practising questions, the students will learn much more from continually revising through spaced practice, and by practising different questions over time, rather than in mock-shaped blocks.

Implication – you can see how this will influence how students make revision notes, and also how you test students in knowledge retrieval tests and cloze exercises, such as the ones I outlined for testing the Knowledge Organiser.

Implication – using these forms of anagrams and words with only first and last letters, or just the opening 2 letters, is incredibly useful in studying essays. If key vocabulary for the whole essay is tested in this way, students won’t just remember the key ideas represented by this vocabulary. They will have a much better recall of the whole essay because of this approach.

So, when asking students to read, we need to shut up. We should only read to students when it is an advantage to do so – for example if the syntax or vocabulary is too complex (which may well be a very frequent occurrence in an ambitious curriculum).

Fortunately, the visual pathway does not interfere with text or speech – so adding diagrams to our resources will help students and not overload them. These diagrams need to inform the text and help students organise or understand the information in it. A picture of a character, for example, is no help at all. A labelled diagram of a character, or of their character arc through the plot, will be much more helpful.

I would also suggest that a way to use spaced learning to learn more from the mocks is to ask students to sit the same questions again at a later date. Only this way can you work out how well they are learning the exam technique of each question. In literature, it will also improve their subject knowledge.

Mind maps synthesise a huge amount of information, but also link it in a way which makes it very memorable. They also provide a ‘big picture’ overview which helps us understand how different elements of a topic interconnect: a schema, in other words.
